newsitem.title: UK: Demand seen pushing aluminium higher by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Demand seen pushing aluminium higher by year-end.

text.p: Aluminium prices could get a modest jolt higher after dozing over the summer if seasonal demand kicks in as expected late this year, analysts said. But the vexed question of stocks complicated the longer term outlook, with analysts divided on whether a recovery would gain enough steam to significantly erode high inventory levels.
"Over the next 18 months I'm largely neutral and we're looking at a market that is roughly in balance," said Angus MacMillan, analyst for broker Billiton.
"We're looking for demand to pick up but not to an extent which will result in a huge drawdown in stocks and that's what you need in order to have a sustained rally in prices," he added.
Aluminium demand has been weaker this year than expected, leading many analysts to revise down their forecasts.

Jim Lennon of Macquarie Equities said he had to change a forecast made at the start of the year of a 2.5 percent rise in 1996 demand to a fall of 0.5 percent and MacMillan sees Western demand falling by 1.5 percent this year.
Many analysts see aluminium demand rising next year by around three percent.
Output is also rising, however, with the huge Alusaf smelter in South Africa, at 490,000 tonnes per year, fully on line and a 193,000-tonne operation in Nigeria seen starting late this year.
MacMillan said he is forecasting a surplus of 300,000 tonnes this year and 200,000 next year, which in a huge market like aluminium, means it is roughly in balance.

Near-term prices may ease further before getting a modest boost toward the end of the year, with MacMillan seeing a higher trading range capped at $1,600 per tonne and broker Rudolf Wolff expecting price to hit $1,700.
Since early June, activity on the aluminium market has been thin with LME three-month prices largely locked in a $1,460-$1,540 range after notching a high of $1,680 on May 9.
Lennon at Macquarie Equities sees consumer destocking as an important factor that should help push prices higher.
Nervous consumers built up stocks in reaction to the rally during 1994 that took prices to a peak of $2,195 in January 1995.

"Since the middle of last year you've seen an end to that restocking and a commencement of quite heavy destocking. We estimate as a rough guide that this year consumer trader stocks have fallen by as much as 250,000 tonnes," Lennon said.
"We're not only expecting a bit of a bounce because underlying economic growth is starting to pick up but also we are looking for a bounce as the destocking ends," he added.
Russian exports is also key to the price equation.
"Russia is likely to find it more and more difficult to export," said analyst William Adams at Wolff.
Production costs are high and domestic consumption should take more supplies, leading to lower exports, he said.
Russian exports in the first half of this year were 300,000 tonnes higher than the same period in 1995, but should decline late this year and in 1997, Lennon said.

But overhanging the market are consignment stocks stored in off-market warehouses -- estimated to total 200,000 to 500,000 tonnes -- by financial institutions who have locked in high forward contangos on the London Metal Exchange, Lennon added.
In the short-term, the market will be eyeing contract negotiations in the United States with the "Big-Three" automakers which expire on September 14.
"Clearly a protracted stoppage would be negative for prices as it would reduce aluminium demand in the short term," broker GNI said in a recent research report.
